questions.q: What is a Git branch, under the hood?
options: A full copy of every file in the repository
A movable pointer to a specific commit
A backup stored on the remote server only
questions.explain: A branch is just a small, movable pointer to one commit — not a duplicate of any files — which is why creating one is nearly instant.

options: The very first commit ever made in the repository
Whichever branch (and commit) you currently have checked out
The author of the most recent commit
questions.explain: HEAD is a pointer that tracks your current position — usually pointing at a branch, which in turn points at a commit.

questions.q: Which command creates a new branch and switches to it in one step?
questions.explain: git switch -c <name> both creates a new branch and immediately switches HEAD to it. git branch alone only creates it, without switching.

questions.q: If main points at commit C, and you create and commit once on a new branch feature-x, what happens to main?
options: main automatically moves forward to the new commit too
main still points at C, unaffected by the new commit on feature-x
questions.explain: Branches are independent pointers. Committing on feature-x only moves feature-x's pointer forward; main keeps pointing at C until something explicitly merges or moves it.

questions.q: What is the older, more overloaded command that git switch and git restore were introduced to replace for most everyday use?
questions.explain: git checkout historically handled both switching branches and restoring files, which was confusing — git switch and git restore split those two jobs apart, though checkout still works and remains common in the wild.
